speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Changi Airport’s excellent connectivity to the world makes Singapore a global city and a vibrant economic hub.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: It also enables Singaporeans to fly to various parts of the world for business and leisure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Unruly passengers can affect the safety of air travel.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: According to International Air Transport Association (IATA), between 2007 and 2016, airlines reported more than 58,000 incidents involving unruly passengers on flights, or about one incident every 1,000 flights.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: There was an increasing number of serious incidents that resulted in injury to air crew or other passengers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: As air travel grows, the problem of unruly passengers may worsen.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Given the importance of civil aviation to Singapore, it is crucial that we uphold Singapore's reputation as a safe and secure aviation hub for all passengers travelling through Changi Airport.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The Montreal Protocol 2014 expands the jurisdictional scope of the Tokyo Convention 1963, which Singapore is a party to, by extending the criminal jurisdiction of a Contracting State to include both the State of landing jurisdiction and the State of the operator jurisdiction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: It will enable Singapore to exercise the State of landing jurisdiction for offences committed on board an aircraft that lands in Singapore, and the State of the operator jurisdiction for offences committed on board an aircraft leased without crew to a lessee whose principal place of business, or whose permanent residence, is in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: These jurisdictions are in addition to the State of registration jurisdiction which enables Singapore to exercise jurisdiction over offences committed on board an aircraft that is registered in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: I will now highlight the key provisions of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Clause 3 enables Singapore to exercise the State of the operator jurisdiction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The definition of "Singapore-controlled aircraft" is revised to include an aircraft that is leased without crew to a lessee whose principal place of business, or whose permanent residence, is in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Clause 4 enables Singapore to exercise the State of landing jurisdiction over offences committed outside Singapore on board an aircraft that is not a Singapore-controlled aircraft, which subsequently lands in Singapore with the offender still on board.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: With this amendment, Singapore can treat any act or omission committed on board an aircraft outside Singapore by an offender who is still on board the aircraft when it lands in Singapore as though it is an offence in Singapore, provided that the act or omission constitutes an offence in Singapore, and take action against the offender accordingly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The commander can also obtain the assistance of a member of the crew, a passenger or an air marshal on board the aircraft in restraining a person whom the commander is entitled to restrain.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: In addition, any crew member, passenger or air marshal on board the aircraft, can, without authorisation of the commander, take measures under the Act against a person on board the aircraft to protect the safety of the aircraft, or persons or property on the aircraft.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Clause 7 accords protection from personal liability to certain persons, for example, the commander of an aircraft, a member of the crew, a passenger or an air marshal, when such persons take action permitted under the Act to protect the safety of the aircraft, or persons or property on the aircraft.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Consequential amendments will be made to the Air Navigation Act and the Police Force Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The Bill will be brought into force in two phases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The provisions establishing Singapore's State of landing jurisdiction will be brought into force after the Bill is passed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This will enhance Singapore's ability to manage incidents of unruly passengers on flights travelling to, through and from Singapore, and give added protection to passengers on these flights before the Montreal Protocol 2014 comes into force.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The remaining provisions will be brought into force on the date the Montreal Protocol 2014 comes into force, which will take place after 22 ratifications have been made.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: If they are on other airlines and land here, they may get off scott-free.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thus, this is a very timely update to the Bill as we continue to tackle the growing issue of unruly passengers on board aircraft.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: That is 51 years later, and a lot of technological changes and also aviation changes have come on since then.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This will now serve as a better, more widespread deterrence and will help to enhance our standing as a safe and secure air hub.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is necessary, as there is substantial air traffic growth every year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: One, this unruly behaviour usually happens not just when airborne.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, in many cases and case studies, it was noted that the negative behaviour commenced even at check-in, at the airport and waiting lounges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thus, how are we training our frontline staff to recognise and take the relevant actions, such as reporting and highlighting these characters and their suspicion?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is also where frontline staff will need to have some communications channel with airport Police and security.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can I ask the Senior Minister of State to help delineate clearly the roles and responsibilities of these different organisations and bodies for the purpose of understanding and clarity?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Which then means there could be no wrong-door policy approach towards reporting and handling the incidences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thirdly, as we move into the future, will the same rules apply to unmanned aircraft, and also what about military customs and Police aircraft?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Fourthly, have there been any case or cases that have arisen in Singapore to date which can be cited as an example where the upgrade to the Montreal Convention will be helpful for us?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In the same context, who will claim extradition, and would extradition law and treaties in existence have to be evoked as well?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The sixth point, on the clause on the powers of the aircraft commander, can the Senior Minister of State clarify, in particular, the role of the aircraft commander ascribed to flights that commence or terminate outside the country of registration?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: With that, Sir, I support the Tokyo Convention (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The incidence of unruly passengers on board aircraft continues to be an important concern in the industry as the number of passenger flights around the world are increasing each year, and, especially with the proliferation of budget airlines all over the world, the safety of passengers and crew on board all passenger aircraft should remain a priority.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have read news of unruly passengers causing flight delays, flight cancellations and even unscheduled landings, not to mention distress and annoyance among crew and passengers on board flights having to put up with unruly behaviour.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The lives and safety of passengers and crew should not be easily put at risk or be endangered by any unruly passenger.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Neither should crew and passengers have to put up with unnecessary delays or inconvenience caused by unruly and unreasonable passengers, unreasonably or wilfully uncompliant with the instructions of the flight commander, that is, the captain, or their crew.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What are the nationalities of such unruly passengers?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How many of these cases would have come under the provisions of this amendment Bill had such provisions been in force earlier?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, while I suppose after the passing of this Bill, Singapore may be able to seize jurisdiction for applicable cases, as the state of landing or as the state of the operator, how would Singapore resolve the conflicts of another jurisdiction wanting to exercise jurisdiction, for example, Singapore can be a state of landing while the state of registration or the state of the operator is another country who also wants to exercise jurisdiction?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Montreal Protocol introduced in the Tokyo Convention the concept of in-flight security officers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under this Bill, we call such "in-flight security officers" by the name "air marshals".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The new section 5(3)(b) under this Bill provides that the aircraft commander may, "request or authorise but not require any ... air marshal to render assistance in restraining any person".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, under this provision, it seems that the aircraft commander does not need to seek the help of air marshals onboard if he does not wish or, presumably, when he thinks that it is not necessary.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, the new proposed section 5(3B) under this Bill also allows an air marshal onboard to take any measures against any person onboard the aircraft without being authorised by the aircraft commander when he has reasonable grounds to believe that such action is necessary.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under the existing unamended section 5, the aircraft commander appears to have the ultimate command or responsibility to take suitable actions during the flight.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The new provisions introduced in Article 6 by the Montreal Protocol and in the proposed amended section 5(3B) stopped short of stating that the air marshals must always defer to the ultimate authority and instruction of the aircraft commander.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will there also be complications affecting states assuming jurisdiction in cases where there is a conflict or disagreement between the aircraft commander and the air marshal?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do we foresee any further changes required to adopt all offences in Circular 288?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Has there been some apprehension, perhaps shared by the many countries which have yet to ratify the Protocol?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: An IATA survey in 2015 also found that handling unruly passengers is one of the key concerns of cabin crew, along with unexpected turbulence and inadvertent slide deployment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As highlighted by the Senior Minister of State, Singapore is a major air transport hub with more than 7,000 weekly scheduled flights.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This means an aircraft takes off or lands at our Changi Airport roughly once every 90 seconds.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is timely, therefore, that our legislation is updated to ensure that flight delays due to unruly passengers are minimised.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Every delay is precious time and resources wasted, affecting not only the airlines, but also passengers and corporations.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The amendments will also serve to ensure the safety of both passengers and cabin crew in a closed environment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Having said that, I would like to seek some clarifications from the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On 9 April last year, United Airlines wanted to bump four passengers off the flight as it was overbooked and Dr David Dao was one of the selected passengers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: He was then forcefully dragged off the plane.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of United Airlines deemed the screaming passenger as "disruptive" and "belligerent" in the initial press release.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In his definition, Dr David Dao was an unruly passenger, though the CEO later issued an apology when the video went viral on social media.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In my view, it is important to have a clear definition of what constitutes “an unruly passenger” and having a clear list of offences or what would be deemed as “unruly behaviour” would certainly be useful to set the out-of-bound (OB) markers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I would like to touch on enhancing training for our aviation workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: According to IATA, the top three factors causing an unruly behaviour inflight are intoxication through alcohol and narcotics, compliance with smoking and other regulation, and disputes between passengers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While cabin crew today are trained to handle unruly behaviour on board the flight, I think training should address the primary causes of unruly behaviour so that we can equip cabin crew to prevent an unruly incident from happening in the first place.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As my colleague, Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef, has mentioned, what about training for ground staff and even retailers at the airport?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can these frontline staff be trained to identify potential “problematic” passengers before they board the plane?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, are food and beverage (F&B) retailers at the airport trained to look out for passengers who already appear to be intoxicated while in transit or while waiting to board?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such a database would allow the airlines to take appropriate precautionary actions against these passengers, including refusal of service.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The database could also serve as a forewarning system for cabin crew and ground staff to pay particular attention to these passengers on board the aircraft.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unruly behaviour, in extreme cases, can threaten the safety of everyone on board the aircraft.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The steady growth in our aviation industry is expected to continue, with Asia as the centre of economic growth in the next decade.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The amendments to this Bill are timely and essential in ensuring the safety and security of both the passengers and our workers in the industry.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The civil aviation sector is a key contributor to Singapore’s economy.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Thus, it is important for us to ensure that Singapore remains a safe and secure air hub.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Government is committed to maintaining high standards of aviation security in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This includes ensuring that aviation security measures are coordinated and consistently applied across the aviation sector.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Civil aviation security policies and implementation of new measures are discussed and decided collectively by a multi-agency committee known as the National Civil Aviation Security Committee, which comprises various Government agencies, such as MOT, the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Singapore Police Force (SPF) and CAAS.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The recommendation for Singapore to ratify the Montreal Protocol 2014 was made by this Committee.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Government agencies also engage with the industry on aviation security issues and measures.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked why did it take four years before we introduced this new amendment Bill.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: That is because there is a need to consult the industry widely.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: At the same time, there is also a timeline for the legislative calendar, and we tried to put this legislation up as soon as possible.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The security measures are implemented by the civil aviation operators, such as Changi Airport Group (Singapore) Pte Ltd, ground handling agents, and the airlines operating in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Compliance with the measures is closely monitored and enforced by SPF.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I agree with Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef and Mr Melvin Yong that the airport staff have a role to play in ensuring the airport and aircraft security in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Government has included all airport personnel, from airport security screeners to check-in counter staff as part of the Threat Oriented Passenger Screening Integrated System (TOPSIS).

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Airport personnel that are in the TOPSIS are trained to look out for and to notify SPF when they detect any passenger displaying suspicious behaviour.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With TOPSIS, airport personnel have become our eyes and ears.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: They support our security agencies in ensuring that Singapore remains a safe and secure environment for air passengers.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked about the incidences of unruly passengers in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: And because they occurred on SIA Group aircraft which are Singapore registered, we have the jurisdiction to actually take action against these unruly passengers.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This is particularly important as most aircraft operated by foreign airlines are not registered in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For example, if an unruly passenger commits an offence on board such aircraft while in airspace outside Singapore en route to Singapore, we will be able to deal with the offender when the aircraft lands in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: There are overseas cases of unruly passenger incidents that have caused disruption to flights to the extent that the pilot decided to divert the plane to land and disembark the unruly passengers.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For example, on 9 September 2016, a British Airways flight from London, the United Kingdom (UK), to Orlando, the United States (US), was forced to land in Boston in the US after a drunk passenger had tried to get off the aircraft in mid-air.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: While interventions had been made by the air stewards and pilot to keep him seated, it was subsequently decided to divert the flight to Boston to deplane the drunk passenger.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef asked who would be punishing the unruly passenger, that is, the state of landing based on where the aircraft lands, the state of registration based on where the aircraft is registered, or the state of nationality based on the nationality of the passenger, or any other jurisdictional bases that are not mentioned here.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Clause 5 of the Bill repeals and re-enacts section 4 to provide for the application of the Extradition Act to offences committed on board an aircraft in flight.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With the change, any offence committed on board an aircraft in flight is treated as if it had been committed not only in the place at which the offence occurred, but also within the countries exercising the state of registration jurisdiction, state of the operator jurisdiction or the state of landing jurisdiction.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Any of these states in whose territory the unruly passenger arrives would be able to take enforcement action to punish him.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Extradition of the unruly passenger can happen when there is an extradition treaty in place between Singapore and the state that is requesting the extradition of the unruly passenger and the requirements under the Extradition Act are satisfied.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked what would constitute as “unruly passenger”.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: ICAO's guidance material on this matter refers to "unruly passengers” as passengers who fail to respect the rules of conduct on board aircraft or to follow the instructions of crew members and thereby disturb the good order and discipline on board aircraft.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: ICAO has provided guidance to identify the incidents which involve various types of offences, ranging from assault on cabin crew or passengers, sexual assault, to illegal consumption of drugs on board the aircraft.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef asked for clarity on the powers of the aircraft commander under the Montreal Protocol 2014.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The aim of doing so is to ensure the safety of the aircraft, other passengers and their properties on board.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Protection of the aircraft commander from personal liability would only apply if the aircraft commander had reasonable grounds to believe that the passenger has either committed an offence or is about to commit an offence or an act which may jeopardise the safety of the aircraft or of persons, property or order and discipline on board.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Training is important to prepare the aircraft commander and the cabin crew in properly assessing the situation and responding to unruly incidents in an appropriate manner.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Airlines have internal guidelines which would prevent unnecessary escalation of a dispute or misunderstanding into a serious unruly incident that would require more serious intervention.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Airlines also have in place training programmes for their cabin crew.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Such programmes equip them with restraint techniques aimed at not imposing unnecessary harm to the unruly passengers as well as to other passengers on board the aircraft.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: IATA has also provided guidance materials to assist their member airlines with the aim of preventing unruly passenger incidents from happening in the first place and to manage them effectively when they do occur.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The guidance provides information on significant risk factors and recommendations to assist in the prevention and management of such events.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked about the role of air marshals.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The air marshal, just like the commander and the other passengers, may also take measures if the air marshal has reasonable grounds to believe that the measures are immediately necessary to protect the safety of the aircraft or persons on board the aircraft from any act of unlawful interference or commission of any serious offence.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, these measures taken by air marshals are subject to any agreement between Singapore and the country that is party to the Montreal Protocol 2014 relating to the deployment of air marshals on board an aircraft for ensuring the safety and security of the aircraft and persons on board the aircraft.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked if it is possible that a common database of unruly passengers be maintained among aviation authorities.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Indeed, some countries that have experienced serious unruly passenger situations have introduced “No-Fly List”.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Montreal Protocol 2014 does not apply to aircraft used in military, Police and customs services.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, we can introduce new or amend legislation if the need arises.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In the area of unmanned aircraft, Singapore is actively participating in international discussions on the issue of security for remotely piloted aircraft systems, including at ICAO.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will continue to ensure that we are ready to protect our aviation system from current and future threats, so as to safeguard our reputation as a safe and secure air hub.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: On the point I raised about the aircraft commander and the air marshal, I am not sure that the Senior Minister of State understood my question correctly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I think I was raising this possibility that there is an element of conflict between the aircraft commander and the air marshal because section 5(3B) stopped short of stating that the air marshal must always defer to the ultimate authority and instruction of the aircraft commander.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: So, I am raising the concern and the question whether there will be complications if there is a conflict or disagreement between the two persons.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: There is one other question I would like the Senior Minister of State to confirm.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Does he foresee there will be any further changes to include further offences which are listed in ICAO's Circular 288 which may not currently be in our Penal Code?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The other question I would like to ask is: how would Singapore deal with the situation when the states of landing – assuming Singapore is the state of landing – the state of landing, the state of the operator or the state of registration, more than one state wants to exercise jurisdiction, how would Singapore, as a state of landing, for example, deal with a situation like this?

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: So, I think there is some understanding whereby the contracting states can decide who should be the country that actually prosecutes the unruly passenger.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I hope I have answered Mr Dennis Tan's queries.
